title: Ramadan: Through the Quran in 30 Days
intro: A verse a day through Ramadan, moving through the Quran roughly in step with the 30 parts (juz) that many Muslims read one a day during the month.

posts.display: The month of Ramadan in which was revealed the Qur'an, a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of the guidance, and the Criterion (of right and wrong).
posts.display_original: شَهْرُ رَمَضَانَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أُنزِلَ فِيهِ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ هُدًى لِّلنَّاسِ وَبَيِّنَٰتٍ مِّنَ ٱلْهُدَىٰ وَٱلْفُرْقَانِ
posts.caption: Ramadan Mubarak. For most Muslims the fast begins around now, though some communities start a day later, depending on the moon. This is the only verse that names the month, linking it with the revelation of the Quran. Through the month, the daily verses move through the Quran roughly in step with its 30 parts (juz), which many Muslims read one a day.

This verse sits in the middle of the Quran's passage on fasting. Asked about Himself, Allah answers by speaking of closeness: "I am nigh". Many Muslims treat the hours of fasting, and the moment of breaking it, as a special time for dua, personal prayer. Pickthall's "suppliant" means one who asks.

Al-Imran ("The Family of Imran") is a Medinan surah. Here the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is told to say that love for Allah shows in following him, and that Allah answers with love and forgiveness. In Ramadan, many Muslims follow his example closely, from rising for suhur, the pre-dawn meal, to breaking the fast with dates.

posts.display: And vie one with another for forgiveness from your Lord, and for a paradise as wide as are the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who ward off (evil).
posts.caption: Al-Imran pictures forgiveness as a race, and Paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth. "Those who ward off (evil)" is Pickthall's phrase for the muttaqin, people of taqwa, God-consciousness. The Quran names taqwa as the purpose of fasting, which makes this verse a natural one for Ramadan.

An-Nisa ("Women") is a long Medinan surah. This verse says no one is wronged by even the smallest amount, while good deeds are multiplied. "The weight of an ant" translates mithqal dharrah, the same phrase rendered "an atom's weight" in Surah Az-Zalzalah. Many Muslims see Ramadan as a season when good deeds count for more.

Later in An-Nisa comes this verse about doing good, openly or in secret, and pardoning a wrong. Pickthall's "Forgiving" here is 'afuww, the One who pardons, from the same root as the verb used for pardoning others. Fasting is often described as a hidden act of worship, known fully only to Allah and the one who fasts.

Al-An'am ("The Cattle") is a Meccan surah about the oneness of Allah. This verse says no eye can take Him in, while He takes in all seeing. Al-Latif, "the Subtle", also carries the sense of gentle and kind, and Al-Khabir, "the Aware", is the One who knows the inner reality of things.

Al-A'raf ("The Heights") is a Meccan surah, and this verse speaks to all the Children of Adam. "Adornment" here means clean, decent clothing for worship. Its middle phrase, eat and drink but without excess, is often recalled at iftar, the meal that breaks each day's fast at sunset.

Near the end of Al-A'raf comes this verse about listening. Many Muslims understand it to apply above all when the Quran is recited in prayer. In Ramadan, many try to read or hear the whole Quran over the month, often in long night prayers in the mosque.

At-Tawbah ("Repentance") is the only surah that does not begin with the Bismillah. After describing the Gardens, this verse names something greater still: ridwan, Pickthall's "acceptance from Allah", meaning His good pleasure. Many Muslims see that as the deepest hope of a month of fasting.

Surah Yunus is a Meccan surah named after the Prophet Yunus (Jonah). Just before this, the Quran calls itself a healing and a mercy. Here it says the bounty and mercy of Allah are worth more rejoicing than anything people hoard, and some commentators read them as Islam and the Quran.

Surah Hud is named after a prophet sent to the ancient Arabian people of 'Ad, and here Hud himself speaks. He links istighfar, seeking forgiveness, with rain, abundance and strength. Many Muslims recall this verse, and a similar one in Surah Nuh, when praying for rain or relief.

Years after losing his son Yusuf (Joseph), and now his youngest too, the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob) sends his sons back to Egypt with this instruction. Pickthall's "Spirit" translates rawh, which also carries the sense of relief and comfort. Even after long grief, the verse refuses despair.

An-Nahl ("The Bee") is a Meccan surah full of the gifts of creation: rain, crops, cattle, honey. This verse sums it up: the favors of Allah are too many to count. For many Muslims, the first sip of water at sunset after a long fast makes the point vividly.

Al-Isra ("The Night Journey") opens the fifteenth juz with the night journey of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ from Mecca to Jerusalem. A few verses on comes this description of the Quran: it guides to "that which is straightest", aqwam, the most upright and balanced way.

In Surah Ta-Ha, these words come to the Children of Israel after their rescue from Pharaoh. "Forgiving" here translates ghaffar, an intensive form meaning ever-forgiving. The verse traces four steps: repenting, believing, doing good and staying on the path.

posts.display: Lo! they used to vie one with the other in good deeds, and they cried unto Us in longing and in fear, and were submissive unto Us.
posts.display_original: إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا۟ يُسَٰرِعُونَ فِى ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ وَيَدْعُونَنَا رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا وَكَانُوا۟ لَنَا خَٰشِعِينَ
posts.caption: Al-Anbiya ("The Prophets") tells how the Prophet Zakariyya (Zechariah) prayed for a child and was given Yahya (John). The verse then describes them: quick to do good, praying "in longing and in fear", raghaban wa rahaban. Hope and awe together are what many Muslims seek in Ramadan prayer.

Al-Mu'minun ("The Believers") is a Meccan surah. These people give generously and still feel afraid. Classical commentators explain that they do good yet worry whether it will be accepted, and that humility keeps them racing toward more good. It is a fitting picture now that Ramadan is past its halfway point.

posts.display: And who spend the night before their Lord, prostrate and standing.
posts.caption: Al-Furqan ("The Criterion") ends with a portrait of 'ibad ar-Rahman, the servants of the Most Merciful, and this is one of its traits. Ramadan nights are known for long prayers, standing in recitation and bowing down in prostration, in mosques and at home.

Al-Qasas ("The Story") is a Meccan surah. This verse follows the story of Qarun, a rich man ruined by his arrogance, and promises the Hereafter to those who seek neither domination nor corruption. For many Muslims, the last ten nights of Ramadan, the most intensely observed, begin around now.

This is the closing verse of Al-Ankabut ("The Spider"), a Meccan surah. Pickthall's "strive in Us" means to strive for the sake of Allah, and the promise is guidance onto many paths. In the last ten nights of Ramadan, many Muslims spend long hours of the night in prayer and reflection.

Al-Ahzab ("The Clans") is a Medinan surah. These two verses call for dhikr, the remembrance of Allah, "much" and "early and late", morning and evening. Many Muslims keep short phrases on their tongues through the day, such as subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar.

Ya-Sin is a Meccan surah that many Muslims recite often. Here sun and moon each keep their own course, and night never outruns day. The Islamic months follow the moon, so Ramadan comes about eleven days earlier each year by the solar calendar, moving through every season over roughly 33 years.

The verse before this one in Az-Zumar tells those who have wronged themselves never to despair of Allah's mercy. This one says what to do with that hope: turn back now, and surrender to Him. In the last ten nights, many Muslims focus especially on asking forgiveness.

posts.display: And He it is Who accepteth repentance from His bondmen, and pardoneth the evil deeds, and knoweth what ye do.
posts.caption: Ash-Shura ("Consultation") is a Meccan surah named for a later verse praising those who settle their affairs by mutual consultation. Here Allah is described as the One who accepts repentance, tawbah, and pardons wrongdoing. Turning back to Allah is one of the great themes of Ramadan's final nights.

posts.display_original: إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَٰهُ فِى لَيْلَةِ ٱلْقَدْرِ وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا لَيْلَةُ ٱلْقَدْرِ لَيْلَةُ ٱلْقَدْرِ خَيْرٌ مِّنْ أَلْفِ شَهْرٍ
posts.caption: Al-Qadr is named for Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, when the Quran was sent down; its worth is "better than a thousand months", over eighty years. Many Muslims seek it especially on the 27th night, which for many begins around this evening; Shia Muslims particularly mark the 19th, 21st and 23rd nights.

Al-Hadid ("Iron") is a Medinan surah. "His slave" is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the revelation is pictured as a way out of darkness into light. In the last nights of Ramadan, many Muslims complete a full reading of the Quran, and many mosques hold a khatm, a completion of the whole recitation.

Al-Hashr is a Medinan surah. This verse frames taqwa, mindfulness of Allah, as looking ahead: each soul is asked to consider what it is sending on for "the morrow", meaning the Hereafter. As Ramadan nears its end, many Muslims take stock of the month in the same spirit.

posts.display: And in whose wealth there is a right acknowledged For the beggar and the destitute.
posts.caption: Al-Ma'arij ("The Ascending Stairways") describes the people of prayer, and among their marks is this: a known share of their wealth belongs to those in need. As Ramadan closes, many Muslims give zakat al-fitr, a small charity given before the Eid prayer so that people in need can share the celebration.

posts.display: But lo! with hardship goeth ease. Lo! with hardship goeth ease.
posts.caption: Ash-Sharh says it twice: with hardship comes ease. Classical commentators noted that "hardship" carries the definite article and "ease" does not, reading it as one hardship met by more than one ease. Ramadan ends around now: for some this is Eid al-Fitr, for others the last fast. Eid Mubarak whenever yours begins, and thank you for reading along.
